title: Your First Script
summary: Write a real script: the #!/bin/sh line, $1, a for loop and $(...).
intro:
A script is a list of commands saved in a file.
Instead of typing the same things again and again, you write them once and run the file.
Today you will build a script line by line that says hello to anyone, and a second one that uses a loop.
outro: You are a script writer now! A shebang line, arguments like $1, a for loop and $(...) are the building blocks of almost every shell script in the world. Try cat greet.sh to admire your work.

steps.instruction: Create a file greet.sh whose first line is #!/bin/sh
hints: echo can write text into a file with >. Put the text in single quotes ' ' so the shell does not change it.
steps.explain: This first line is called the shebang (say 'sha-bang'). It tells the computer which program should run the script. Here it is /bin/sh, the standard shell.

steps.instruction: Add this line to the end of greet.sh: echo "Hello, $1!"
hints: Use >> to ADD a line (one > would replace the whole file!). Put single quotes on the outside and keep the double quotes inside.
steps.explain: $1 is the first word you give the script when you run it. The single quotes kept $1 as plain text in the file, so it gets its value later, when the script runs. Peek at your file with cat greet.sh

hints: You did this in the last lesson, with chmod.
steps.explain: Now greet.sh has the x permission, so you can start it like a real program with ./greet.sh

steps.instruction: Run your script and give it your name, for example ./greet.sh Ank
hints: Write your name after the script name, with a space in between.
steps.explain: The word after the script name became $1. If you add more words, the second one is $2, the third is $3, and so on. Try ./greet.sh world too!

steps.instruction: Time for a loop! Create a script list.sh that prints 'Text file: ' and the name of every .txt file. Then run it with sh list.sh
hints: A loop looks like this: for f in *.txt; do echo "Text file: $f"; done   Save that line into list.sh with echo and single quotes.
Type: echo 'for f in *.txt; do echo "Text file: $f"; done' > list.sh   and then: sh list.sh
steps.explain: for repeats a command once for each item. *.txt became notes.txt and todo.txt, and f took each name in turn. The jpg files were left out. Also notice: sh list.sh runs a script even without the x permission.
steps.solution:
echo 'for f in *.txt; do echo "Text file: $f"; done' > list.sh
sh list.sh

steps.instruction: Make greet.sh smarter: add a line that prints 'Today is ' and the day of the week. Use $(date +%A) for the day. Then run ./greet.sh with your name again.
hints: $(command) puts the output of a command inside your text. date +%A prints the weekday, like Monday. Single quotes on the outside again!
Type: echo 'echo "Today is $(date +%A)"' >> greet.sh   and then: ./greet.sh Ank
steps.explain: $(...) is called command substitution: the shell runs the command inside and pastes its output into the text. Your script asks the computer for the day every time it runs. That's the magic of scripts: commands saved in a file, ready whenever you need them.
